The Spotted Owl (Strix occidentalis) attains a maximum total length of 48.3 centimeters [Li = 48.3 centimeters], a size typical of medium-to-large forest owls in the Pacific Northwest. This ultimate length is realized only after several years of growth, as individuals continue to add skeletal mass even after reaching reproductive maturity. In terms of body mass, substantial sexual dimorphism is evident within the Mexican subspecies, with adult females achieving a peak wet weight of 680 grams [Wwi = 680 grams] while the heaviest recorded adult males reach 625 grams [Wwi = 625 grams]. These values represent the upper extremes of the reported ranges and likely reflect individuals in prime condition within high-quality territories. The pronounced difference in mass between the sexes is characteristic of many strigiforms and is thought to relate to the female's role in egg production and the energetics of extended incubation periods.

Eggs laid by female Spotted Owls weigh approximately 48.85 grams [Wwb = approximately 48.85 grams] at oviposition, a substantial investment given that each clutch typically contains two eggs. This neonatal wet weight is derived from egg dimensions averaging 50.62 millimeters in length and 42.93 millimeters in breadth, yielding a calculated fresh mass of about 48.85 grams. The incubation period itself, measured under controlled conditions at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts an average of 30 days [ab = 30 days] before hatching commences. This duration is somewhat protracted compared to smaller northern owls, a pattern consistent with the allometric scaling of incubation length with egg size and body mass. The thermal environment of the nest cavity, which typically remains near 36 °C, is crucial for normal embryonic development and the synchronization of hatching across the brood.

Under optimal conditions in mature forests, clutch size is fixed at 2 eggs per breeding event [N_R_i = 2 eggs per breeding event], with breeding occurring exactly once per year [F_R_i = once per year], a rate that severely constrains the species' intrinsic rate of increase and makes population recovery slow after disturbance. Females do not produce replacement clutches if the initial nest fails in most years, further constraining annual reproductive success. Fledging success is highly variable and depends on prey abundance, with individuals in low-quality territories often failing to raise any young to independence. The combination of small clutch size and low reproductive frequency renders the Spotted Owl particularly vulnerable to habitat fragmentation and reductions in prey availability.

The maximum recorded lifespan in captivity for a Spotted Owl is quite exceptional, with the oldest documented individual surviving for 25 years [am = 25 years] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan greatly exceeds the typical mean observed in wild populations, which generally ranges from 15 to 17 years, reflecting the hazards of predation, disease, and food scarcity in natural environments. The remarkable captive longevity, likely achieved under the stable thermal and nutritional conditions characteristic of a carefully managed environment at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], underscores the species' slow life-history pace. This extended potential lifespan, combined with delayed reproduction and low annual fecundity, places Strix occidentalis firmly among the most slow-living of the larger forest owls, a strategy that is only viable in stable, mature forest ecosystems with reliable prey bases. Senescence and age-related physiological decline become apparent after two decades.
